title: ImageDoctor: Diagnosing Text-to-Image Quality via Grounded Reasoning
one_liner: Instead of scoring images with one number, ImageDoctor gives four separate quality scores plus pixel maps showing exactly where the image went wrong.
lead: When you generate an image from text, how do you know if it is good? Today's models usually give one score: 0.7 or 0.8 or something. That single number hides what actually broke. ImageDoctor changes that by giving four scores at once (plausibility, semantic alignment, aesthetics, overall) and highlighting the exact pixels that misbehaved. When you use ImageDoctor to steer training, images get 10 percent better because the model can now target fixes to the exact regions and dimensions that failed, instead of blindly adjusting to a single opaque score.

problem.h2: One number cannot tell the whole story
paras: When you want to train a text-to-image model to be better, you need a judge to rate the results because training needs a signal to know which direction to change the weights. That judge looks at a generated image and a prompt and asks: is this good? Right now, the judge gives back one score: a number between 0 and 1, because the goal is to distill a complex judgment into a single number for easy ranking.

A beginner tries to use that single score to steer training. But a score of 0.6 could mean the image is blurry, or it means the dog has three legs, or it means the colors are ugly, or all three at once. The model cannot tell which flaw to fix because the feedback is a black box. You get a low score, but you do not know what to change.

callout.html: ImageDoctor replaces a single quality score with four separate scores plus pixel-level maps showing exactly which parts of the image misbehaved.

steps.text: The judge receives the generated image and the text it came from.
The model scans the image to spot regions that do not match the prompt.
For each flagged region, the model explains what went wrong in plain text.
Plausibility, semantic alignment, aesthetics, overall quality, plus pixel flaw indicators.
The four scores and heatmap guide the model to fix specific problems.

paras: ImageDoctor changes what the reward signal looks like. Instead of one scalar reward (a single number), it outputs four scores plus spatial heatmaps. This gives training a dense, interpretable signal: not just how good the image is, but which parts broke and why.

hidden.name: flaw localization
paras: Flaw localization is the spatial map of which image pixels disagreed with the prompt. It is hidden because you cannot see it in the final image; you have to infer it by comparing the image to what the text asked for. ImageDoctor estimates this by having a vision-language model (a model trained to read both images and text at once) look at the image and reason about which regions are implausible or misaligned.

The paper measures flaw localization as a heatmap: each pixel gets a strength score (0 to 1) indicating whether it is part of a flaw. The model generates this heatmap by first identifying regions that deviate from the prompt, then producing text explanations, then turning those explanations into numerical quality scores that correspond to pixel regions.

heat.caption: Darker cells indicate pixels where the model detects flaws; lighter cells pass inspection.

reads.html: The heatmap is a picture where brighter areas are okay and darker areas show trouble. A pixel gets darker if the vision-language model judges that region to be implausible or misaligned with the prompt.

ImageDoctor produces pixel-level flaw indicators via its reasoning process: the model first localizes regions of concern, generates textual reasoning, then produces quantitative scores at the image patch level. These patch-level scores form the heatmap that serves as dense reward.

mechanism.h2: Why changing the reward structure improves images
paras: Dense, localized feedback trains faster and more accurately than a single global score because it tells training not just that something is wrong, but exactly where and how to fix it. Here is the causal chain: when training steers an image model, it needs to know not just how wrong the output was, but where the mistake is and what kind of mistake it is. A single score of 0.6 tells you nothing. Four scores (plausibility, alignment, aesthetics, overall) already narrow the problem: if alignment is 0.3 but the others are high, you know to fix semantic match. Adding a pixel-level heatmap narrows it further: now training can see which exact regions caused the low alignment score.

This matters because gradient-based training (the nudges that reshape the model weights) works best when the signal is specific and local. If you tell training the dog has three legs (a specific flaw at pixels X, Y, Z), training can directly modify the circuitry that generated pixels X, Y, Z. If you just say the image is bad, training has to guess. Specificity shortens training and reduces trial-and-error. The reasoning step (look, think, predict) helps because it forces the model to articulate what it saw before scoring, creating intermediate supervision that makes the final score more honest.

stages.s: Generates text explanation of each flaw
Produces four scores and pixel heatmap
Training updates weights to reduce heatmap regions

math.words: The loss for training the image model incorporates four weighted quality scores plus a penalty for high-confidence flaw regions. The total loss combines the mismatch between the generated image and human preference, scaled by how much each dimension (plausibility, alignment, aesthetics, overall) deviates from ideal, plus a term that penalizes generating pixels in regions flagged by ImageDoctor as flawed.
math.equation: loss = w_p * (1 - plausibility_score) + w_a * (1 - alignment_score) + w_e * (1 - aesthetics_score) + w_o * (1 - overall_score) + lambda * mean(heatmap)
symbols: weights controlling how much each dimension matters
how realistic the image looks (0 to 1)
how well the image matches the text (0 to 1)
how visually appealing the image is (0 to 1)
pixel-level flaw indicators (0 to 1 per pixel)
how strongly to steer toward no flaws
average flaw strength across all pixels

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an image gets plausibility_score=0.8, alignment_score=0.4, aesthetics_score=0.7, overall_score=0.65.
Suppose w_p=1, w_a=2, w_e=1, w_o=1 (alignment weighted doubly), lambda=1, and mean(heatmap)=0.3.
Now suppose the next version improves alignment to 0.6: alignment_score=0.6, mean(heatmap)=0.2 (fewer flaws).
Loss dropped from 2.35 to 1.85 because the model improved both alignment and flaw density. Training rewards both.

math.note: The loss combines four separate quality judgments plus pixel-level flaw pressure. Training reduces all of them together, steering images toward human preference across multiple dimensions.

charts.title: Scalar reward (one number)
charts.note: One score hides which dimension failed, so training wastes iterations guessing.

charts.title: ImageDoctor (four scores plus heatmap)
charts.note: Four scores plus heatmap make problems explicit, so training fixes them faster and more completely because the model can directly update the circuits responsible for each specific flaw instead of making blind adjustments.

items.html: If the underlying vision-language model has learned incorrect associations (e.g., it thinks all dogs must be brown), it will flag brown dogs incorrectly. The heatmap inherits the model's biases.

If the reasoning text does not actually match the flaw regions, or if the model learns to generate plausible-sounding excuses rather than true analysis, the scores become meaningless. This can happen if the reasoning is not directly supervised against ground truth explanations.

If the heatmap is computed at a coarse patch level but training updates happen at fine pixel resolution, the dense reward may not actually guide gradients to the right weights. The spatial alignment between heatmap and training updates must be precise.

ImageDoctor works when the vision-language backbone is strong and unbiased, the reasoning step is trained on real human explanations, and the heatmap resolution matches the training granularity. In that case, images improve steadily and human raters agree with the four scores because the dense reward signal aligns training incentives with what humans actually value across all four dimensions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a text-to-image model (or use a pretrained one) and train it on a small dataset using two reward models: (1) a scalar-only baseline that outputs one quality score, and (2) ImageDoctor with four scores and heatmaps. Show that after the same number of training steps, ImageDoctor-trained images score higher on all four dimensions and that human raters prefer them.
demo.closing: If the demo is set up correctly, you will see ImageDoctor images improve 10 percent faster and reach higher final quality because the dense pixel-level reward prevents the model from getting stuck in local minima when only one dimension is weak.
